facts.statement: The genus Carcharodontosaurus was established by Ernst Stromer in 1931.
facts.quote: authority: Stromer, 1931

facts.statement: A partial skeleton was discovered in Egypt in 1914 by crews working for Ernst Stromer, who reported the find in 1931.
facts.quote: A partial skeleton was discovered in Egypt as early as 1914 by crews of German paleontologist Ernst Stromer, although he did not report the find until 1931.

facts.statement: C. saharicus reached approximately 12 meters in length and 5 to 7 metric tons in body mass, making it one of the largest known theropods.
facts.quote: C. saharicus reached around 12 m in length and approximately 5 - 7 MT in body mass, and was therefore one of the largest theropod dinosaurs known.

facts.statement: Its jaws contained sharp, recurved, and serrated teeth resembling those of the great white shark, which inspired the genus name.
facts.quote: Its jaws were lined with sharp, recurved, and serrated teeth that bear striking resemblances to those of the great white shark (genus Carcharodon), the inspiration for the name.

facts.statement: Two teeth were unearthed in 1924 from wall cuts near Timimoun in French Algeria.
facts.quote: In 1924, two teeth of Carcharodontosaurus were unearthed from wall cuts in different foggaras near Timimoun, French Algeria.

facts.statement: In 1925, Depéret and Savornin described the teeth as a new species, Megalosaurus saharicus.
facts.quote: In 1925, Depéret and his colleague Justin Savornin described the teeth as coming from a new species of theropod dinosaur, Megalosaurus saharicus.

facts.statement: A partial skeleton was first found near Ain Gedid, Egypt, in April 1914 by Richard Markgraf.
facts.quote: However, a partial skeleton later assigned to C. saharicus was first found in marls near Ain Gedid, Egypt, in early April 1914 by Austro-Hungarian paleontologist Richard Markgraf.

facts.statement: The skeleton was transported to Munich in 1922 and described by Stromer in 1931.
facts.quote: It was not until 1922 that they were transported overseas to Munich, where they were described by Stromer in 1931.

facts.statement: In 2025, the main skeleton was redescribed as the holotype of a distinct genus, Tameryraptor.
facts.quote: However in 2025, this specimen was redescribed as the holotype of a distinct carcharodontosaurid genus, Tameryraptor.

facts.statement: Many fossils from French expeditions in North Africa were assigned to Carcharodontosaurus based on limited information, a classification now questioned.
facts.quote: This led many fossils of carcharodontosaurids found during French geologic expeditions to North Africa to be assigned to Carcharodontosaurus based on little information and traits now found in other genera.

facts.statement: A 2012 study suggests all isolated teeth previously assigned to Carcharodontosaurus from North Africa are indeterminate due to the presence of other genera in the region.
facts.quote: with a 2012 study by American researcher Matthew Carrano and colleagues stated that all isolated Carcharodontosaurus teeth from the North Africa could only be considered indeterminate carcharodontosaurid teeth due to the presence of other carcharodontosaurid genera in the region.

facts.statement: It is debated whether postcranial fossils from the Elrhaz Formation belong to Carcharodontosaurus or a different taxon, as the postorbital resembles Acrocanthosaurus.
facts.quote: French paleontologist Philippe Taquet noted that the postorbital was similar to that of Acrocanthosaurus, another carcharodontosaurid, suggesting it may be from Carcharodontosaurus however the postcranial fossils could belong to a different taxon.

facts.statement: Teeth from the Gara Samani Formation were identified as Carcharodontosaurus but may instead belong to abelisaurids.
facts.quote: Additionally, from the Gara Samani Formation, previously a part of the Continental intercalaire, have been identified as Carcharodontosaurus teeth, however they may belong to abelisaurids instead.

facts.statement: An incomplete skull of Carcharodontosaurus was discovered in 1995 by American paleontologist Paul Sereno.
facts.quote: Few discoveries of Carcharodontosaurus attributed material were made until 1995 when American paleontologist Paul Sereno found an incomplete skull during an expedition embarked on by the University of Chicago.

facts.statement: The type skull was found in Cenomanian-aged rocks of the Lower Douira Formation in southeastern Morocco.
facts.quote: This skull was found in the Cenomanian-aged rocks of the Lower Douira Formation, Kem Kem Beds, in Errachidia, southeastern Morocco.

facts.statement: The presence of Carcharodontosaurus in the Kem Kem Beds was first suggested in 1954 by René Lavocat based on fragmentary fossils.
facts.quote: The presence of Carcharodontosaurus in this formation was first suggested in 1954 by French palaeontologist René Lavocat on the basis on fragmentary fossils.

facts.statement: The skull catalogued as SGM-Din 1 was initially described in 1996 by Sereno and colleagues in the journal Science.
facts.quote: The skull, since catalogued as SGM-Din 1 at the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Environment in Rabat, Morocco, was first taken to the University of Chicago, where it was initially described in 1996 by Sereno and colleagues in Science.

facts.statement: In 2007, specimen SGM-Din 1 was proposed as the neotype of C. saharicus because the original lectotype teeth were lost.
facts.quote: In 2007, SGM-Din 1 was officially proposed as the neotype (replacement type specimen) of C. saharicus due to the loss of the lectotype teeth and the similar age and geographic location to previously noted material.

facts.statement: The species C. iguidensis was described in 2007 by Steve Brusatte and Paul Sereno.
facts.quote: In 2007, another species of Carcharodontosaurus, C. iguidensis, was described by American paleontologists Steve Brusatte and Paul Sereno.

facts.statement: Fossils of C. iguidensis were found in the Echkar Formation near Iguidi, Niger.
facts.quote: Fossils of C. iguidensis had been uncovered during an expedition to the rock layers of Iguidi, Niger, then identified as part of the Echkar Formation.

facts.statement: A 2016 study suggested that most material assigned to C. iguidensis actually belongs to other genera, leaving only the holotype valid.
facts.quote: However, a 2016 paper by Italian researchers Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza and Andrea Cau identified the non-holotypic material of C. iguidensis as belonging to Sigilmassasaurus and a non-carcharodontosaurine, and therefore chose to limit C. iguidensis to the holotype pending future research.

facts.statement: A 2025 study proposed that C. iguidensis represents a distinct genus separate from C. saharicus.
facts.quote: A 2025 abstract presented by British paleontologist Charlie Scherer and colleagues at the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology annual meeting stated that C. iguidensis is from a distinct genus of carcharodontosaurid due to anatomical, phylogenetic, and biogeographic differences with C. saharicus.

facts.statement: The validity of the genus Sauroniops is debated, with some researchers considering it a synonym of C. saharicus or a dubious taxon.
facts.quote: Sauroniops validity has been questioned by several papers, with some stating that it is dubious (a species lacking diagnostic features) or a synonym of C. saharicus.

facts.statement: Giganotosaurus was synonymized with Carcharodontosaurus in 1998 and 2010, but this classification has not been accepted by subsequent authors.
facts.quote: The South American genus Giganotosaurus was synonymized with Carcharodontosaurus in 1998 by Brazilian author Silvério Domingues Figueiredo and in 2010 by American paleontologist Gregory S. Paul, but no authors have since followed this assessment.

facts.statement: French geologist Hugues Faure collected isolated Carcharodontosaurus-like teeth from the Akarazeras site in the Farak Formation.
facts.quote: The authors also recalled French geologist Hugues Faure's collection of isolated Carcharodontosaurus-like teeth from the Akarazeras site of the Farak Formation.

facts.statement: A maxillary tooth from the Villar del Arzobispo Formation in Spain was assigned to Carcharodontosaurus in 1966.
facts.quote: A maxillary tooth recovered from the Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Spain was assigned to Carcharodontosaurus in 1966.

facts.statement: The Spanish tooth assigned to Carcharodontosaurus lacks typical carcharodontosaurid traits and resembles other allosauroids.
facts.quote: However, it lacks the traits of carcharodontosaurid teeth and instead is more similar to that of other allosauroids.

facts.statement: Teeth from Brazil have been placed in Carcharodontosaurus, but this assignment is disputed due to geographic origin and lack of diagnostic features.
facts.quote: Teeth from the Alcantara Formation and the Itapecuru Group of Brazil have placed in Carcharodontosaurus, but this has been disputed based on its geographic origin and lack of diagnostic features.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Wadi Milk Formation in Sudan were once compared to Carcharodontosaurus but are now considered indeterminate carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Several vertebral centra (base of vertebrae), a tarsal (bone in the heel), a metatarsal (foot/ankle bone), and a pedal phalanx from Wadi Milk Formation of Sudan were compared Carcharodontosaurus, but were now considered to be indeterminate carcharodontosaurids, some of which are similar to the genus.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Quseir Formation in Egypt have been tentatively assigned to both Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus but remain classified as indeterminate.
facts.quote: Fossils from the Campanian Quseir Formation of western Egypt have been tentatively assigned to Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus, but these specimens were never described in detail and thus classified as indeterminate.

facts.statement: The neotype of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was estimated to be 12 to 12.5 meters long and weigh 5 to 7 metric tons.
facts.quote: The latter was estimated to be 12 - 12.5 m in length and approximately 5 - 7 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis reached a maximum length of 10 meters and a body mass of 4 metric tons.
facts.quote: C. iguidensis was much smaller, only reaching 10 m in length and 4 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: In 1996, Paul Sereno and colleagues estimated the skull of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus to be 1.60 meters long.
facts.quote: In 1996, Paul Sereno and colleagues estimated the skull of C. saharicus to be 1.60 m

facts.statement: In 2007, François Therrien and Donald M. Henderson estimated Carcharodontosaurus to be 13.3 meters long and 15.1 metric tons in weight.
facts.quote: In 2007, Canadian researcher François Therrien and American researcher Donald M. Henderson found that Giganotosaurus would have approached 13 m in length and 13.8 MT in weight, while Carcharodontosaurus would have approached 13.3 m in length and 15.1 MT in weight

facts.statement: The neotype skull of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus would measure 1.6 meters when complete.
facts.quote: The neotype skull of C. saharicus would measure 1.6 m when complete

facts.statement: Sculpted exteriors on the maxillae are a diagnostic trait unique to the genus Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus skull has sculpted exteriors on its maxillae, which is a trait unique to the genus.

facts.statement: There are 14 tooth sockets present in each maxilla of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus.
facts.quote: 14 teeth sockets are present in each maxilla.

facts.statement: A recent estimate suggests Carcharodontosaurus had a total of 62 teeth: 30 in the dentary, 8 in the premaxilla, and 24 in the maxilla.
facts.quote: Estimations of the tooth count of Carcharodontosaurus vary, but a recent estimate of 30 dentary, 8 premaxillary, and 24 maxillary teeth for a total of 62 teeth was made.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus had over 18 to 20 serrations per centimeter of tooth edge, while C. iguidensis had up to 32 per centimeter.
facts.quote: Serrations are numerous on the anterior and posterior margins, with over 18 to 20 serrations per centimetre of edge in C. saharicus and up to 32 per centimetre in C. iguidensis.

facts.statement: The teeth of Carcharodontosaurus are straight and spindle-shaped in cross-section.
facts.quote: The teeth are straight and spindle-shaped in cross-section.

facts.statement: Since the mid-1990s, there has been a debate among researchers regarding whether Tyrannosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, Giganotosaurus, or Spinosaurus was the largest theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: Debate over what was the largest theropod dinosaur has ensued since the mid-1990s, with different researchers arguing that Tyrannosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, Giganotosaurus, or Spinosaurus was the largest theropod.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno and Rodolfo Coria agreed that settling the size contest between Carcharodontosaurus and Giganotosaurus was difficult and less important than studying other aspects of these dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Sereno countered that it would be difficult to determine a size range for a species based on few, incomplete specimens, and both paleontologists agreed that other aspects of these dinosaurs were more important than settling the "size contest".

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus was a robust theropod with small forelimbs, an elongated tail, and a short neck.
facts.quote: Like other carcharodontosaurids, it was robust with small forelimbs, an elongated tail, and short neck.

facts.statement: Canadian researcher Dale A. Russell assigned a single cervical vertebra to the genus Carcharodontosaurus in 1996.
facts.quote: A single cervical vertebra was assigned to the genus by Canadian researcher Dale A. Russell in 1996.

facts.statement: The preserved length of the cervical vertebra assigned to Carcharodontosaurus by Russell is 148 mm.
facts.quote: Its preserved length is 148 mm.

facts.statement: Cau and colleagues tentatively assigned another incomplete cervical vertebra to Carcharodontosaurus in 2025 based on its stratigraphic and geographic position.
facts.quote: Another incomplete cervical vertebra was tentatively assigned to the genus by Cau and colleagues (2025) on the basis of its stratigraphic and geographic position.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus is the type genus of the family Carcharodontosauridae and the subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus is the type genus of the family Carcharodontosauridae and subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae.

facts.statement: The family Carcharodontosauridae was originally created by Stromer for Carcharodontosaurus and Bahariasaurus, but the name was not used until the late 20th century.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosauridae was a clade created by Stromer for Carcharodontosaurus and Bahariasaurus, though the name remained unused until the recognition of other members of the group in the late 20th century.

facts.statement: Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues defined the group Carcharodontosauridae in 2004 as all allosauroids closer to Carcharodontosaurus than to Allosaurus or Sinraptor.
facts.quote: The group was defined as all allosauroids closer to Carcharodontosaurus than Allosaurus or Sinraptor by the American paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues in 2004.

facts.statement: Kellermann, Cuesta, and Rauhut suggested in 2025 that C. iguidensis belongs to a different genus because it is a non-carcharodontosaurine member of Carcharodontosauridae outside the genus Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: In the phylogenetic analyses of their 2025 paper, Kellermann, Cuesta and Rauhut recovered C. iguidensis as a non-carcharodontosaurine member of the Carcharodontosauridae outside the genus Carcharodontosaurus, suggesting that this species belongs to a different genus.

facts.statement: The genus Carcharodontosaurus was named by Stromer in 1931.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Stromer, 1931

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Carcharodontosaurus is Carcharodontosaurus saharicus.
facts.quote: type_species: Carcharodontosaurus saharicus

facts.statement: The type species Carcharodontosaurus saharicus was named by Depéret and Savornin in 1927.
facts.quote: type_species_authority: Depéret & Savornin, 1927

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis was named by Brusatte and Sereno in 2007.
facts.quote: subdivision: Carcharodontosaurus iguidensis Brusatte & Sereno, 2007

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus fossils range from the Early to Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Inferior-Superior

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus lived in the middle of the Cretaceous period, approximately 100 million years ago, between the Albian and Cenomanian stages, extending a few thousand years into the early Turonian, in what is now Africa.
facts.quote: que vivieron a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 100 million years ago, entre el Albianense y Cenomaniense llegando unos pocos miles de años hasta inicios del Turoniense, en lo que hoy es África.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus was one of the largest known predatory dinosaurs and shared its territory and time with Spinosaurus, another large carnivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: Es uno de los mayores dinosaurios predadores que se conocen, y compartió el mismo territorio y la misma época con Spinosaurus, otro dinosaurio carnívoro de gran tamaño.

facts.statement: Estimates for the length and weight of C. saharicus range from 12 to 12.5 meters and 6 tons, respectively.
facts.quote: Las diferentes estimaciones de longitud y peso de la especie C. saharicus oscilan entre 12 a 12.5 metros de longitud y entre las 6 toneladas de peso.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus had one of the largest skulls observed in terrestrial animals, approximately 1.60 meters long.
facts.quote: Tenía uno de los mayores cráneos de los observados hasta ahora en animales terrestres, de aproximadamente 1,60 metros de largo

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus had serrated teeth similar to those of sharks, which functioned to tear flesh, causing prey to bleed out.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus tenía mandíbulas llenas de aserrados dientes parecidos a los de los tiburones (de ahí su nombre «lagarto con dientes de tiburón»), que tenían la función de desgarrar carne, por lo que sus presas morían desangradas

facts.statement: Fossil tracks suggest Carcharodontosaurus could run at speeds up to 8.5 m/s (around 30 km/h), though this estimate is now debated.
facts.quote: Tenían como todo Carnosauria unas largas y musculosas patas traseras, y rastros fosilizados indican que podían correr hasta 8,5 m/s (alrededor de 30 km/h), aunque ahora dicha estimación es objeto de controversia.

facts.statement: Despite its size, the bite force of Carcharodontosaurus was not very high, being easily surpassed by Tyrannosaurus rex and slightly by Giganotosaurus, but similar to or greater than that of Spinosaurus.
facts.quote: A pesar del tamaño del animal, la fuerza mandibular de Carcharodontosaurus no era muy alta, siendo superada fácilmente por Tyrannosaurus rex y ligeramente por Giganotosaurus pero similar o mayor a la de Spinosaurus.

facts.statement: A study by Donald Henderson suggests Carcharodontosaurus could physically lift animals weighing up to 424 kilograms with its jaws.
facts.quote: Un estudio realizado por Donald Henderson, conservador de dinosaurios en el Museo Tyrrell, sugiere que Carcharodontosaurus fue capaz de levantar físicamente con sus mandíbulas animales que pesaban un máximo de 424 kilogramos.

facts.statement: The description of other North African carcharodontosaurids like Tameryraptor and Sauroniops has questioned the assignment of remains lacking overlap with the C. saharicus neotype to Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: However, the description of other carcharodontosaurids from North Africa such as Tameryraptor and Sauroniops has put into question the referral of carcharodontosaurid remains that lack overlap with the C. saharicus neotype.

facts.statement: Oliver Rauhut's 1995 analysis of Carcharodontosaurus systematics was based on material now assigned to Tameryraptor.
facts.quote: In a 1995 paper, German researcher Oliver Rauhut analyzed the systematics of Carcharodontosaurus—though this was based on the material now assigned to Tameryraptor—and Bahariasaurus.

facts.statement: Later studies have not supported Rauhut's conclusions, suggesting Bahariasaurus is a ceratosaur, "A." tendagurensis is an indeterminate tetanuran, and "M." ingens is possibly a species of Torvosaurus.
facts.quote: However, later studies have not supported these conclusions, with Bahariasaurus being suggested to be a ceratosaur, "A." tendagurensis being an indeterminate tetanuran, and "M." ingens possibly being a species of Torvosaurus.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus was discovered by French paleontologists Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus fue descubierto por los paleontólogos franceses Charles Depéret (1854-1929) y Justin Savornin (1876-1970).

facts.statement: The discovery took place in North Africa in 1924.
facts.quote: El descubrimiento tuvo lugar en el norte de África en 1924

facts.statement: German paleontologist Ernst Stromer von Reichenbach described partial remains of a skull and parts of the skeleton in 1931.
facts.quote: En 1931, el paleontólogo alemán Ernst Stromer von Reichenbach describió los restos parciales de un cráneo y partes del esqueleto

facts.statement: The remains consisted of a partial skull, teeth, vertebrae, claw bones, and classified hip and hind leg bones.
facts.quote: Los restos consistían en un cráneo parcial, dientes, vértebras, huesos de una garra y también los huesos clasificados de la cadera y de una pata trasera.

facts.statement: The first discovered Carcharodontosaurus fossil was destroyed in Allied bombing raids on Germany during World War II.
facts.quote: El primer fósil de Carcharodontosaurus en haber sido descubierto fue destruido en los bombardeos que los aliados llevaron a cabo sobre Alemania durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

facts.statement: A more complete new skull was found in the Kem Kem Formation of Morocco during an expedition led by paleontologist Paul Sereno in 1995.
facts.quote: Un nuevo cráneo más completo fue encontrado en la formación Kem Kem de Marruecos durante una expedición dirigida por el paleontólogo Paul Sereno en 1995

facts.statement: This new specimen of C. saharicus is the largest found of its species and genus, with a skull measuring 1.6 meters in length.
facts.quote: Este nuevo espécimen de C. saharicus es el más grande hallado de su especie y género y solo su cráneo mide 1,6 metros de largo

facts.statement: Its estimated size was between 12 and 12.8 meters in length and about 6.2 tons in weight.
facts.quote: se estima que su tamaño fue de entre 12 y 12,8 metros de longitud y su peso en unas 6,2 toneladas.

facts.statement: Sereno and Stephen Brusatte reported a second species found in Niger in 2005, named C. iguidensis in 2007, which differs in some aspects of the maxilla and skull base.
facts.quote: El mismo Sereno y Stephen Brusatte en 2005 reportaron una segunda especie que fue encontrada en Níger, que difiere en algunos aspectos del maxilar y de la base del cráneo, llamada C. iguidensis en 2007.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimates that C. iguidensis measured 10 meters in length and weighed 4 tons.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estima que C. iguidensis medía 10 metros de largo y pesaba 4 toneladas.

facts.statement: Remains were found in Cenomanian rocks of the Baharija Formation in Egypt.
facts.quote: provenientes de rocas del Cenomaniano de la formación Baharija de Egipto

facts.statement: Remains and teeth assigned to C. saharicus have been found in much of Africa.
facts.quote: Restos y dientes asignados a C. saharicus han sido encontrados en gran parte de África

facts.statement: Remains of C. iguidensis have only been found so far in the Echkar Formation, west of the In Abangharit oasis, in the Iguidi area of Niger.
facts.quote: los restos de C. iguidensis solo han sido encontrados hasta ahora en la formación Echkar, al oeste del oasis In Abangharit, en el área conocida como Iguidi, en Níger.

facts.statement: Originally, in 1925, Depéret and Savornin attributed the binomial name Megalosaurus saharicus to their specimen.
facts.quote: Originalmente, en 1925, Depéret y Savornin atribuyeron a su espécimen el nombre binominal Megalosaurus saharicus

facts.statement: The specimen was later attributed by the same authors to the genus Dryptosaurus.
facts.quote: Más tarde fue atribuido por los mismos autores al género Dryptosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2001, Hans C. E. Larsson published a description of the inner ear and endocranium of C. saharicus.
facts.quote: En 2001, Hans C. E. Larsson publicó una descripción del oído interno y el endocráneo de C. saharicus.

facts.statement: The midbrain is inclined downward at an angle of 45 degrees and toward the rear of the animal.

facts.statement: Carcharodontosaurus also had a large optic nerve.
facts.quote: Carcharodontosaurus también tenía un nervio óptico grande.

facts.statement: The three semicircular canals of the inner ear of C. saharicus, viewed from the side, had a subtriangular outline.
facts.quote: Los tres canales semicirculares del oído interno de C. saharicus, vistos desde el lado, tenían un contorno subtriangular.

facts.statement: This subtriangular inner ear configuration is present in Allosaurus, lizards, and turtles, but not in birds.
facts.quote: Esta configuración subtriangular del oído interno está presente en Allosaurus , lagartos, tortugas, pero no en aves.

facts.statement: The semicircular canals were actually very linear, which explains the pointed silhouette.
facts.quote: Los canales semicirculares eran en realidad muy lineales, lo que explica la silueta puntiaguda.

facts.statement: It is debated whether this new specimen of C. saharicus is the largest found of its species and genus, as it is stated as a fact in the source but implies a comparison with previous incomplete knowledge.
facts.quote: Este nuevo espécimen de C. saharicus es el más grande hallado de su especie y género
